about.title: Fairfield Product Liability Claims
about.longDescription: A space heater that overheats in a Fairfield kitchen, a tire that separates on I-80 near the Air Base Parkway exit, a child's car seat that fails during a stop on Travis Boulevard — defective products reach Solano County households the same way they reach everywhere else: through ordinary shopping. What sets these cases apart is how California treats them. Under strict product liability, you usually do not have to prove the manufacturer was careless. You show the product had a design, manufacturing, or warning defect, and that the defect caused your injury. That shifts a great deal of the burden off you and onto the companies that made, distributed, and sold the item. Fairfield's 112,970 residents share roads that recorded 645 injury collisions and 912 injured people in 2025, and some of those crashes involve airbags, brakes, or seatbelts that did not perform as designed. LawProactive is a free service, not a law firm. We connect you with an independent attorney who works on contingency, so keep the product, keep the packaging, and reach out when you are ready.

whyChoose.title: Why Fairfield Residents Turn to LawProactive

items.title: Strict liability shapes the case
items.desc: In California, you generally need to show the product was defective and that the defect caused your injury — not that anyone was negligent. The attorney we connect you with builds the claim around that standard from day one.

items.title: Evidence starts with the product itself
items.desc: The heater, the tire, the car seat — whatever hurt you is the single most important piece of evidence. We connect you quickly so an attorney can advise you on preserving it before it is discarded or repaired.

items.title: More than one company may answer
items.desc: Manufacturers, distributors, and retailers can each be held responsible under California law. An independent attorney can identify every party in the chain, which matters when one of them is out of state or hard to reach.

items.question: My airbag did not deploy in a crash on I-80 in Fairfield. Could that be a product liability claim?
items.answer: It might be, alongside any claim against another driver. If the airbag, seatbelt, or braking system did not perform the way it was designed to, the vehicle or component maker may be strictly liable for the injuries that failure caused or made worse. Do not have the car repaired or salvaged until an attorney has had a chance to look at it. Fairfield sees a steady volume of crashes on I-80 and Air Base Parkway, and vehicle defects are sometimes overlooked in the rush to settle with an insurer.

items.question: Do I have to prove the company knew the product was unsafe?
items.answer: Usually not. California's strict liability rule focuses on the product, not the company's state of mind. If the item had a design flaw, a manufacturing error, or lacked proper warnings, and that defect injured you, the claim can proceed without proving negligence. Your attorney will evaluate which type of defect applies to your situation.

items.question: I already threw away the product that hurt me. Is my claim over?
items.answer: Not necessarily, though it does make things harder. Photos, receipts, packaging, medical records, and the same model purchased elsewhere can sometimes fill the gap. If you still have any part of the product, stop using it and store it as-is. An attorney connected through LawProactive can tell you what evidence is realistic to recover.
